rows.reference: Seneca, Letters to Lucilius 95.51 to 95.53 (Gummere's Loeb numbering as in Perseus: 'Ut pareamus sanguini humano?' in 95.51; 'membra sumus corporis magni' and 'miserius est nocere quam laedi' both in 95.52; 'Homo sum' in 95.53)
rows.original: Ut pareamus sanguini humano? Quantulum est ei non nocere, cui debeas prodesse! ... membra sumus corporis magni ... miserius est nocere quam laedi
rows.translation: Latin of Gummere's Loeb edition (Perseus), read directly; English is my own close rendering; Gummere's English (1925) not read in this pass
rows.says: On how human beings are to be treated: what precept do we give? That we spare human blood? How little it is not to harm someone you ought to help. All that is divine and human is one; we are limbs of one great body. Nature made us kin and gave us love for one another. By her law it is more wretched to harm than to be harmed, and our hands should be ready to help.
rows.bearing: Rule 7: a duty owed to every human being, grounded in shared kinship, so it reaches everyone K1 and K0 protect (strangers, slaves, wrongdoers). Sparing human blood is named as the least that is owed to anyone. Explicit wider rule for K1 and K0. It does not name newborns and cannot remove a contradicting counted text (rule 2; De Ira 1.15.2).

rows.reference: Seneca, Letters to Lucilius 95.30 to 95.31 and 95.33 (Perseus numbering)
rows.original: Homicidia compescimus et singulas caedes; quid bella et occisarum gentium gloriosum scelus? ... Homo, sacra res homini, iam per lusum ac iocum occiditur
rows.translation: Latin of Gummere's Loeb edition (Perseus), read directly; English is my own close rendering; Gummere's English not read in this pass
rows.says: Our madness is public as well as private. We restrain murders and single killings, but what of wars and the 'glorious crime' of slaughtering whole peoples? What is forbidden to private persons is ordered by decrees of the senate and people; deeds that would cost a man his life if done in secret are praised when generals do them. Humans, the gentlest of kinds, are not ashamed to delight in each other's blood and to hand wars on to their children. A human being, a sacred thing to human beings, is now killed for sport in the arena.
rows.bearing: K1 and K0: murder is treated as plainly wrong and every human being is called 'a sacred thing' to others; Explicit wider rule. K3: Clear teaching through a wider rule: the killing of war, and above all the slaughter of whole peoples (which takes in children, the old and other non-combatants), is called a crime. This is the main counted text for K3. War is context only for K1 (rule 5). The arena victims in 95.33 were condemned people and captives (context: court), but the principle is stated of every human being.
rows.strength: Explicit (wider rule) for K1 and K0; Clear teaching (wider rule) for K3

rows.reference: Seneca, De Ira 2.31.6 to 2.31.8 (Latin Library numbering)
rows.original: foedam esse et execrabilem uim nocendi et alienissimam homini ... Nefas est nocere patriae; ergo ciui quoque ... ergo et homini, nam hic in maiore tibi urbe ciuis est ... homines singulis parcent quia ad coetum geniti sunt
rows.translation: Latin (The Latin Library text, CLTK copy), read directly; English is my own close rendering; Aubrey Stewart (1889) not read in this pass
rows.says: Above all, think that the power to harm is foul, accursed and most alien to a human being. It is wrong to harm your country, so it is wrong to harm a fellow citizen, and so it is wrong to harm any human being, who is your fellow citizen in the greater city. As the limbs of a body agree because each one's safety matters to the whole, so people will spare each individual, because they are born for community. We would not even kill vipers if we could tame them; so we will not harm even a human being because he has done wrong, but so that he will not do wrong. Punishment looks to the future, not the past.
rows.bearing: Explicit wider rule (rule 7) against harming any human being, directly against limiting protection to one's own community, and reaching wrongdoers. 2.31.8 rejects harm in return for a past wrong, so it also supports K0's revenge clause. Its account of punishment is context (rule 5). It does not remove De Ira 1.15.2 (rule 2).

rows.original: Homo in adiutorium mutuum genitus est, ira in exitium ... hic etiam ignotis succurrere
rows.translation: Latin (The Latin Library text, CLTK copy), read directly; English is my own close rendering; Aubrey Stewart (1889) not read in this pass
rows.says: What is gentler than a human being in a right state of mind, what crueller than anger? A human being is born for mutual help, anger for destruction; one seeks company, the other separation; one wants to do good, the other harm; one helps even strangers, the other attacks even those dearest. Human life rests on kindness and concord, bound together by mutual love, not by terror.
rows.bearing: Clear teaching for K0's anger clause, with a wider teaching that human nature is for mutual help, even of strangers. It describes human nature and anger rather than stating a rule about killing, so Clear teaching, not Explicit.

rows.original: Inhumanum uerbum est et quidem pro iusto receptum ultio
rows.translation: Latin (The Latin Library text, CLTK copy), read directly; English is my own close rendering
rows.says: It is said that anger is pleasant and that paying back pain is sweet. Not so: it is honourable to repay kindness with kindness, but not wrongs with wrongs. 'Revenge' is an inhuman word, though accepted as just; the one who returns pain differs from the first wrongdoer only in coming second. Cato, struck by mistake in the baths, said he did not remember being struck: it was better to ignore than to avenge. It is the mark of a great mind to despise wrongs.
rows.bearing: Explicit for K0's revenge clause, as a wider rule against all revenge, which includes revenge killing (rule 7). It also governs how De Ira 1.12 ('uindicabit', 'exequar') is read within Seneca's own treatise.

rows.reference: Seneca, De Ira 3.12.4 to 3.12.7 (Plato and his slave)
rows.original: Nihil tibi liceat dum irasceris. Quare? quia uis omnia licere.
rows.translation: Latin (The Latin Library text, CLTK copy), read directly; English is my own close rendering
rows.says: The greatest remedy for anger is delay. Plato, angry with a slave, held his raised hand still and said he was punishing an angry man; then he handed the slave to Speusippus to correct, saying 'I am angry; I would do more than I ought'. Should anyone entrust revenge to an angry man, when Plato took power away from himself? Let nothing be permitted to you while you are angry, because then you want everything to be permitted.
rows.bearing: Explicit for K0's anger clause as a wider rule (rule 7): nothing at all is to be done in anger, which includes killing. The example is a master and his slave, so it binds heads of households. The punishment in the story is a flogging, not a killing.

rows.original: Numquid amplius isti cui irasceris quam mortem optas? etiam te quiescente morietur ... colamus humanitatem; non timori cuiquam, non periculo simus
rows.translation: Latin (The Latin Library text, CLTK copy), read directly; English is my own close rendering
rows.says: What more do you wish on the one you are angry with than his death? He will die even if you do nothing. 'I do not want to kill him, only to exile, shame or fine him': whether you think of the ultimate penalty or lighter ones, how short is the time of his pain or of your evil joy. While we are among human beings, let us cultivate humanity; let us be a cause of fear or danger to no one.
rows.bearing: Clear teaching for K0's anger and revenge clauses: wishing and seeking the death of the person you are angry with is argued against, and the closing rule ('a danger to no one') is a wider duty reaching everyone (rule 7).

rows.original: aequi bonique natura, quae parcere etiam captivis et pretio paratis iubet ... est aliquid, quod in hominem licere commune ius animantium vetet ... O hominem mille mortibus dignum
rows.translation: Latin (The Latin Library text, CLTK copy, and Perseus), read directly; English is my own close rendering; Aubrey Stewart (1889) not read in this pass
rows.says: Ruling slaves with moderation is praiseworthy. With a slave, ask not how much he can suffer without penalty, but what the nature of fairness and goodness allows, which bids us spare even captives and those bought with money. Though the law permits everything against a slave, the common law of living beings forbids some things against a human being. Everyone hated Vedius Pollio, who fattened his lampreys on human blood and had slaves who had offended him thrown into his fishpond: a man who deserved a thousand deaths. Cruel masters are pointed out and detested in the whole city.
rows.bearing: Rule 7, taught in part: Clear teaching that a master's killing of slaves for offending him is condemned whatever the law allows, on the ground of shared humanity, and that nature 'bids us spare' slaves. The text says only that 'some things' are forbidden; it does not state a rule that a master may never kill a slave. Also bears on K0 (killing from cruelty or anger at an offence). The phrase about captives is Implied only for K3, because its context is slaves, not war.

rows.original: Fregerat unus ex seruis eius crustallinum; rapi eum Vedius iussit ... murenis obici ... saeuitia erat ... Si calix tuus fractus est, uiscera hominis distrahentur?
rows.translation: Latin (The Latin Library text, CLTK copy), read directly; English is my own close rendering; Aubrey Stewart (1889) not read in this pass
rows.says: Rebuking an angry man only provokes him, unless you have the standing of Augustus. Dining with Vedius Pollio, Augustus saw Vedius order a slave who had broken a crystal cup to be thrown to his huge lampreys: it was cruelty. The boy escaped to Caesar's feet, asking only to die some other way. Moved, Caesar had him let go, had all the crystal broken in front of him and the pond filled in, and asked: 'If your cup is broken, shall a man's entrails be torn apart?' Seneca says Caesar used his power well.
rows.bearing: Clear teaching (rule 7, taught in part): a master's killing of a slave in anger over a trivial loss is condemned, through a story the teacher expressly approves ('bene usus est uiribus suis'). Augustus acts with a ruler's authority, but what is condemned is a private master's killing, so rule 5 does not remove it. Supports K0 (anger) and K1 for slaves. (3.40.1 suggests calming an angry friend by telling him the offender 'will pay' later; this is advice on handling an angry person, not a teaching that revenge is right.)

rows.reference: Seneca, De Clementia 1.15.1 (the knight is Tricho in both local texts)
rows.original: Trichonem equitem Romanum memoria nostra, quia filium suum flagellis occiderat, populus graphiis in foro confodit
rows.translation: Latin (The Latin Library text, CLTK copy, and Perseus), read directly; English is my own close rendering; Aubrey Stewart (1889) seen by search in an earlier session
rows.says: Within living memory, because the Roman knight Tricho had flogged his son to death, the people stabbed him with their writing styluses in the Forum; the authority of Augustus barely rescued him from the hands of fathers and sons alike. Seneca gives this as an example of how cruelty earns hatred.
rows.bearing: Taught in part (rule 7) for children in a father's power: a father's lethal cruelty is presented as hateful, against any reading of Roman paternal power as a licence to kill. The condemnation is voiced through the people's reaction and Seneca's frame, so this is at the lower edge of Clear teaching. The crowd's attack is reported, not approved (rule 4). It does not address newborns and does not answer De Ira 1.15.2.

rows.original: Non unum est imperandi genus; imperat princeps civibus suis, pater liberis, praeceptor discentibus, tribunus vel centurio militibus ... nulli magis parcendum
rows.translation: Latin (The Latin Library text, CLTK copy), read directly; English is my own close rendering
rows.says: Let no one be so cheap to a king that he does not notice when that person dies. There is more than one kind of rule: a prince rules citizens, a father his children, a teacher his pupils, an officer his soldiers. A father who beats his children constantly for trivial causes is the worst of fathers; a teacher who tortures his pupils is unworthy. No creature needs more skill to handle than a human being, and none is more to be spared. It is foolish to be ashamed of venting anger on beasts and dogs and yet let a human being under a human being be in the worst condition.
rows.bearing: Clear teaching through a wider rule for those under any authority: fathers, teachers and officers, not only rulers, must spare and treat gently those in their power, because no creature is more to be spared than a human being. Supports K1's reach to heads of households and K0's anger clause. It is about harsh treatment, not killing as such, so it supports rather than decides.

rows.original: οὔτε ὀργίζεσθαι τῷ συγγενεῖ δύναμαι οὔτε ἀπέχθεσθαι αὐτῷ ... τὸ οὖν ἀντιπράσσειν ἀλλήλοις παρὰ φύσιν
rows.translation: Greek (Leopold, Teubner 1908, in Perseus), read directly; English is my own rendering; George Long (1862), the project's translation, seen by search in an earlier session
rows.says: Each morning, expect to meet meddling, ungrateful, insolent, deceitful, envious and unsocial people; they are so through ignorance of good and evil. The wrongdoer is my kin, sharing not blood or seed but mind and a portion of the divine. I cannot be harmed by them, nor be angry with my kinsman or hate him. We are made to work together, like feet, hands and eyelids, so to act against one another is contrary to nature.
rows.bearing: Rule 7: a wider duty not to act against any other person, reaching everyone and naming wrongdoers ('the wicked' in K1). Clear teaching for K1 (wider rule) and, through 'not angry, not hate', for K0. It does not mention killing, newborns or defence.

rows.original: Ἴδιον ἀνθρώπου φιλεῖν καὶ τοὺς πταίοντας
rows.translation: Greek (Leopold, Teubner 1908, in Perseus), read directly; English is my own rendering; Long (1862) not read in this pass
rows.says: It is proper to a human being to love even those who stumble. This comes if you remember that they are your kin, that they do wrong through ignorance and unwillingly, that soon you will both be dead, and above all that they have not harmed you, for they have not made your ruling mind worse than it was.
rows.bearing: Clear teaching for K0's hatred and revenge clauses and for K1's reach to wrongdoers (rule 7).

rows.original: οὐκ ἀνέξῃ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ τοῦ σαυτοῦ, ὃς ἔχει τὸν Δία πρόγονον ... εὐθὺς τύραννον καταστήσεις σεαυτόν; ... ἀλλʼ ὠνὴν αὐτῶν ἔχω ... εἰς τοὺς ταλαιπώρους τούτους νόμους τοὺς τῶν νεκρῶν
rows.translation: Greek (Schenkl, Teubner 1916) and George Long's English (his 1877 translation, Bell printing of 1887), both in Perseus, read directly
rows.says: When a slave does not bring the warm water you asked for, or brings it lukewarm, not to be angry or burst out is pleasing to the gods. Slave yourself, will you not bear with your own brother, who has Zeus for his forefather? If you are placed above others, will you at once make yourself a tyrant? Remember whom you rule: kinsmen, brothers by nature, offspring of Zeus. 'But I bought them, and they did not buy me.' You are looking to the earth, to the pit, to these wretched laws of the dead, and not to the laws of the gods.
rows.bearing: Clear teaching through a wider rule, supporting K0: a master must not treat those in his power with anger or as a tyrant, because every human being is kin, and ownership under human law does not change this. Implied only for K1, since killing is not mentioned.
rows.strength: Clear teaching (wider rule, supporting) for K0; Implied for K1

rows.reference: Epictetus, Discourses 1.18.3 to 1.18.12 ('That we ought not to be angry with wrongdoers')
rows.original: τοῦτον οὖν τὸν λῃστὴν καὶ τοῦτον τὸν μοιχὸν οὐκ ἔδει ἀπολωλέναι; ... γνώσῃ πῶς ἀπάνθρωπόν ἐστιν ὃ λέγεις ... ἐλέει αὐτὸν μᾶλλον ἢ μίσει
rows.translation: Greek (Schenkl, Teubner 1916) and George Long's English, both in Perseus, read directly
rows.says: Thieves and robbers are mistaken about good and evil: should we be angry with them or pity them? Show them their error and they will stop. 'Ought not this robber and this adulterer to be destroyed?' Put it rather: ought not this man, deceived and blinded about the greatest things, to be destroyed? Then you will see how inhuman your words are, as if one asked whether a blind or deaf man should be destroyed. Pity him rather than hate him; drop this readiness to take offence and to hate. If you did not prize your clothes or your wife's beauty, you would not be angry with the thief or the adulterer.
rows.bearing: Clear teaching that wrongdoers, the robber and the adulterer among them, are not to be hated or 'destroyed' for their error: supports K1's reach to 'the wicked' and K0's anger and hatred clauses. Epictetus speaks of attitude and does not discuss legal penalties (context, rule 5).

rows.original: τῷ θυμῷ χαρίσασθαι καὶ τιμωρήσασθαι τὸν ἄνδρα, συμφορώτερον ἡγεῖται τοῦ σῶσαι τὰ τέκνα ... ἐξηπάτηται ... ἔχις ἀντὶ ἀνθρώπου γέγονεν
rows.translation: Greek (Schenkl, Teubner 1916) and George Long's English, both in Perseus, read directly
rows.says: Medea judged that gratifying her anger and taking revenge on her husband was more to her advantage than saving her children. She was deceived; show her plainly and she will not do it. Why be angry with the wretched woman, who has gone astray about the greatest things and become a viper instead of a human being? Pity her, as we pity the blind and the lame. Whoever remembers this will be angry with no one and hate no one.
rows.bearing: Clear teaching that killing one's own children for revenge springs from a false judgement and is a grave wrong (she 'became a viper instead of a human being'): supports K0's revenge clause and K1 for children. Epictetus answers with pity, not anger. Medea is a figure of drama, but the teacher judges the act, so rule 4 does not reduce it.

rows.reference: Seneca, De Beneficiis 7.20.1 to 7.20.2 (the tyrant's infant son)
rows.original: Servabo filium eius infantem; quid hoc beneficium obest cuiquam eorum, quos crudelitas eius lacerat?
rows.translation: Latin (Perseus), read directly; English is my own close rendering; Aubrey Stewart (1887) not read in this pass
rows.says: Even with a tyrant who has forfeited every claim, Seneca keeps a measure in what he will do for him: 'I will save his infant son: how does this benefit harm any of those whom his cruelty tears apart?' He will not give him money for guards or soldiers.
rows.bearing: Clear teaching, in part, that the child of the worst wrongdoer keeps his protection: the infant is to be saved even when his father has lost all claim. Supports K1's protection of children and of the families of 'the wicked'.

rows.original: Servi sunt. Immo homines ... sic cum inferiore vivas, quemadmodum tecum superiorem velis vivere
rows.translation: Latin of Gummere's Loeb edition (Perseus), read directly; English my own (translations.md flags Gummere's word 'betters'); Gummere's English seen by search in an earlier session
rows.says: 'They are slaves.' No, they are human beings, companions, humble friends, fellow slaves of fortune. We make enemies of them by treating them not even as human beings but as beasts of burden. The one you call your slave was born of the same seeds, enjoys the same sky, breathes, lives and dies as you do. Live with those below you as you would want those above you to live with you.
rows.bearing: Implied for K1 and K0: shared humanity and the Golden Rule applied to people in one's power rule out killing them only by an argument (no one wishes to be killed), not by plain teaching. Does not decide.

rows.original: Errat, si quis existimat servitutem in totum hominem descendere ... nulli sceleri manus commodabunt ... de iniuriis dominorum in servos qui audiat positus est ... Immo homo ab homine
rows.translation: Latin (Perseus), read directly; English is my own close rendering; Aubrey Stewart (1887) not read in this pass
rows.says: Virtue is open to all, free, freed and slave. It is a mistake to think slavery reaches the whole person: the body is bound to the master, the mind is free. Slaves will not obey orders against the state or lend their hands to any crime. A slave can receive a wrong from his master, and an official has been appointed to hear masters' wrongs against slaves and to restrain their cruelty, lust and meanness. Does a master receive a benefit from a slave? Rather, a human being from a human being.
rows.bearing: Implied for K1: slaves are persons who can be wronged by their masters, masters' cruelty is a public concern, and no one under orders may lend his hands to a crime. It does not mention killing.

rows.reference: Seneca, De Ira 1.15.1 to 1.15.3 (the decisive clause is 1.15.2; Latin Library numbering)
rows.original: tollantur e coetu mortalium ... sed hoc sine odio ... portentosos fetus extinguimus, liberos quoque, si debiles monstrosique editi sunt, mergimus; nec ira sed ratio est a sanis inutilia secernere
rows.translation: Latin (The Latin Library text, CLTK copy), read directly; English is my own close rendering; Aubrey Stewart (1889), the project's translation, was seen only through search in an earlier session
rows.says: Wrongdoers should be corrected by warning and by force, gently and harshly, but without anger. Those who cannot be corrected should be removed from the company of mortals, but without hatred: no one hates his own limbs when he cuts them off; it is not anger but a wretched cure. We kill mad dogs, slaughter a fierce untamable ox, put the knife to diseased sheep so they do not infect the flock; we destroy monstrous births, and our children too, if they are born weak and deformed, we drown. It is not anger but reason to separate the useless from the sound. Nothing suits one who punishes less than anger.
rows.bearing: K1: Contradicted (rules 2, 5 and 9). Newborns are persons for K1 (rule 9). The decisive clause is 'liberos quoque ... mergimus' (our children too we drown): in Seneca's list it is an act of parents and households, not a court's sentence, so exclusion (a) does not cover it (rule 5). Seneca does more than report a custom: 'nec ira sed ratio est' classes it as reason, which for a Stoic is right action, and he uses it as a model for right punishment, so rule 4 does not apply. No branches, so rule 2, not rule 3. Points for reviewers: (i) the sentence is one of several analogies in an argument about removing incorrigible wrongdoers (1.15.1), which is itself context (rule 5); (ii) 'portentosos fetus extinguimus' may refer to the public expiation of prodigies, and some modern scholars connect the drowning with it (outside the corpus); on that reading the act would be by public order, not on a parent's own authority. No Stoic counted text, commentator or authority gives either reading, so rule 6 does not apply as written. K0: hard case (rule 6). The stated motive is expressly not anger ('nec ira') nor hatred ('sine odio'), and in Seneca's frame the purpose is to keep the sound from harm (the flock analogy); whether ridding a household of a child judged 'useless' is killing 'for your own gain' is unresolved. The passage also supports K0's anger and hatred clauses.

rows.reference: Seneca, De Beneficiis 7.19.5 to 7.20.4 (a benefactor who has become a tyrant)
rows.original: intercisa iuris humani societas abscidit ... omnia mihi in illum libera sint ... ut nihil in eum nefas esset ... eadem manu beneficium omnibus dabo, illi reddam; quoniam ingeniis talibus exitus remedium est
rows.translation: Latin (Perseus), read directly; English is my own close rendering; Aubrey Stewart (1887) not read in this pass
rows.says: Must I repay a benefit to a man who has become a savage tyrant like Apollodorus or Phalaris? If he is wicked only within himself, I repay it, to be quit of him. But if he feeds on human blood, tortures people of every age from a lust for cruelty, cuts children's throats before their parents' eyes, and his citadel is always wet with fresh blood, then the bond of human law that tied him to me is cut. From then on everything is permitted to me against him; by corrupting all right he has made it that nothing done to him is wrong. Yet I will keep a measure: I will repay only a benefit that does not strengthen him for the common ruin; I will save his infant son; I will not give him money for guards or soldiers. And if his cure is wholly despaired of, with the same hand I will give a benefit to all and repay it to him, since for such natures death is the remedy, and it is best for one who will never return to himself to depart. Such wickedness is rare, a portent.
rows.bearing: Approves, as a benefit to all, a private person's bringing about the death of a tyrant who is actively killing and torturing and cannot be cured. That fits the exception in K1 and K0 (stopping someone from killing or gravely harming others), and the condition 'if his cure is wholly despaired of' stands in for necessity. The wider words 'nothing done to him is wrong' come close to declaring the tyrant outside all protection (rule 2), but the only killing approved is under the exception, and Seneca still limits what he will do (he will save the infant son). Read so, it is a limit, not a contradiction. If the project lead reads 'nihil in eum nefas' as a forfeiture of protection by status, it is a hard case (rule 6); K1 is already Contradicted by De Ira 1.15.2, and for K0 the motive is the good of all and the tyrant's 'remedy', not gain, anger, hatred or revenge, so no label changes.

rows.original: Dedit aliquis domino suo vitam, dedit mortem ... primum dominum occidit ... Da mihi quemquam, qui magnificentius dominum servaverit
rows.translation: Latin (Perseus), read directly; English is my own close rendering
rows.says: Among examples of benefits slaves have given their masters: one gave his master life, one gave him death, one saved him by dying. Vettius, a commander of the Marsi, was being led as a prisoner to the Roman general; his slave drew the sword of the soldier escorting him, killed his master first, said 'Now it is time to see to myself: I have already freed my master', and killed himself with one blow. Seneca: show me anyone who saved his master more magnificently. (3.23.3, in another story, mentions a mistress's 'power of life and death' over her slaves.)
rows.bearing: A counted text approving a private person's deliberate killing of another person (a slave, acting on his own initiative) as a benefit to the victim. The setting is war (exclusion (b)), and the act is a death given to spare a captive from his enemies, close to voluntary death and mercy killing (exclusion (d)); the text does not say whether Vettius asked for it. So it is a hard case for K1 (rule 6), not a clear contradiction; K1 is already Contradicted by De Ira 1.15.2, so no label changes. For K0, the motive is the master's supposed good, not gain, anger, hatred or revenge, so it does not cut against K0. The 'power of life and death' in 3.23.3 is presupposed, not approved (rule 4).

rows.reference: Seneca, De Ira 1.12.1 to 1.12.5 (with De Ira 3.15.2)
rows.original: Non irascetur, sed uindicabit, sed tuebitur ... Pater caedetur: defendam; caesus est: exequar, quia oportet, non quia dolet
rows.translation: Latin (The Latin Library text, CLTK copy), read directly; English is my own close rendering
rows.says: 'Will a good man not be angry if he sees his father struck down or his mother carried off?' He will not be angry, but he will avenge (or punish) and protect. 'My father is being struck: I will defend him; he has been struck: I will follow it up, because it is right, not because it hurts.' To be angry for one's own is weakness; what is fine is to come forward as defender of parents, children, friends and fellow citizens, led by duty, willing, judging and foreseeing. (Similarly, De Ira 3.15.2 does not forbid a father whose children a king had killed to condemn the deed and 'seek a penalty worthy' of it.)
rows.bearing: Defending one's father and others fits K1's exception; this is the only counted text found that names defence of others as a duty. 'caedi' may mean struck or slain, and 'uindicare' and 'exequi' may mean private vengeance or pursuit through the courts; neither passage names a killing. Seneca's own treatise rejects revenge as 'an inhuman word' (De Ira 2.32.1) and harm for a past wrong (2.31.8), so within the counted texts 'exequar' is best read as pursuing the matter without anger, not as a revenge killing. Implied at most as approval of revenge; it does not decide or unsettle K0. It supports K0's anger clause.

rows.original: Quid properamus uerberare statim, crura protinus frangere? non peribit potestas ista, si differetur ... ad ferrum uenimus, ad capitalia supplicia
rows.translation: Latin (The Latin Library text, CLTK copy), read directly; English is my own close rendering
rows.says: What a great thing we will have done if we send an unhappy slave to the workhouse! Why do we rush to flog him at once, to break his legs straight away? That power will not be lost if it is put off. Wait until we give the order ourselves, not anger. Here above all we go wrong: we resort to the sword and to capital punishments, and punish with chains, prison and hunger a matter that deserved a few light lashes.
rows.bearing: No killing is approved, so it does not decide K1 or K0. It shows protection graded by status for bodily harm: a master's punishment of a slave, even breaking his legs, is treated as within his power ('non peribit potestas ista'), and only haste and anger are faulted. 3.32.2 faults resorting 'to the sword and to capital punishments' for small faults: it presupposes, without approving, punishments up to death (rule 4). Supports K0's anger clause.

rows.original: τολμᾷ λέγειν ὅτι μὴ ἀναιρώμεθα τέκνα. ἀλλὰ πρόβατον μὲν οὐκ ἀπολείπει τὸ αὑτοῦ ἔγγονον οὐδὲ λύκος, ἄνθρωπος δʼ ἀπολείπει; ... οὐκ ἄν σε ἔρριψαν
rows.translation: Greek (Schenkl, Teubner 1916) and George Long's English, both in Perseus, read directly
rows.says: Epicurus knows that once a child is born we cannot help loving and caring for it, yet he dares to say we should not raise children. A sheep does not abandon its young, nor does a wolf; shall a human being? Who would follow you on seeing his own child fallen and crying? Even if your mother and father had been told that you would say this, they would not have cast you away.
rows.bearing: The strongest counted Stoic text against getting rid of children: abandoning one's offspring is against nature, and 'casting away' is the word used of exposure. For K1 it is Implied, since it speaks of raising and abandoning, not killing, and it does not address weak or deformed infants. It opposes De Ira 1.15.2 in spirit but does not narrow it (rule 6 needs a reading that limits the hard text; this one does not touch it), so K1 stays Contradicted under rule 2.

rows.original: Quam rationem in occidendo secutus sit, alias tractabimus; mihi enim ... in hac re videtur vehementer errasse nec ex institutione Stoica se egisse
rows.translation: Latin (Perseus), read directly; English is my own close rendering
rows.says: It is debated whether Brutus should have accepted his life from Julius Caesar when he judged that Caesar ought to be killed. 'What reasoning he followed in the killing I will discuss elsewhere.' Seneca thinks Brutus, a great man in other ways, went badly wrong here and did not act on Stoic teaching: he feared the name of king, though the best state is under a just king, and hoped for a freedom that could not return.
rows.bearing: Faults Brutus's political judgement and says his course was not Stoic, while expressly setting aside the question of the killing itself. Implied only. A narrow counterweight to Cicero, De Officiis 3.19 and 3.32 (Tier 2). It sits beside De Beneficiis 7.19 to 7.20, which approves a tyrant's death only for a tyrant who is actively killing and past cure.

rows.reference: Seneca, De Clementia 1.14.1 to 1.14.3 and 1.15.2 to 1.15.7 (a father's household court; Tarius)
rows.original: Nemo ad supplicia exigenda pervenit, nisi qui remedia consumpsit ... contentus exsilio et exsilio delicato Massiliae ... Non culleum, non serpentes, non carcerem decrevit
rows.translation: Latin (The Latin Library text, CLTK copy, and Perseus), read directly; English is my own close rendering; Aubrey Stewart (1889) seen by search in an earlier session
rows.says: A good parent scolds, warns and sometimes beats his children; no sane father disinherits a son for a first offence; he tries everything first and takes up the decisive pen only when the case is hopeless. 'Let a father be slow to cut off his own limbs.' Tarius found his son plotting parricide, tried him after hearing the case in a family council attended by Augustus, and was content with exile, a comfortable exile at Massilia with the same allowance as before. Augustus proposed not the sack, the serpents or prison (the parricide penalties) but that a father should be content with the mildest penalty. Everyone admired Tarius.
rows.bearing: A father's household court sits between a court and private authority (rules 5 and 6), but it decides nothing: the text approves exile, not killing, and names disinheritance as a father's last step; it presupposes, without approving any lethal use of, a father's power to judge his son (rule 4). Supports clemency in households.

rows.original: ultima supplicia sceleribus ultimis ponat, ut nemo pereat nisi quem perire etiam pereuntis intersit ... interim optimum misericordiae genus est occidere ... nemo prudens punit quia peccatum est, sed ne peccetur
rows.translation: Latin (The Latin Library text, CLTK copy), read directly; English is my own close rendering
rows.says: Punishment is like medicine: the guardian of the laws and ruler of the state should use words first, then harsher words, then light and revocable penalties, and the ultimate punishment only for the ultimate crimes, so that no one dies unless his death is good even for him. 'The good man does no harm' (Plato). The magistrate will condemn and order executions without anger, with the face of the law; sometimes killing is the best kind of mercy. No wise person punishes because a wrong was done, but so that it will not be done; the power of life and death must not be given to an angry man.
rows.bearing: Punishments by courts and rulers are context only (rule 5). Shows that counted Stoic texts accept capital punishment by public authority while requiring that it be without anger, a last resort and for prevention. 'Interim optimum misericordiae genus est occidere' (1.16.3) is said of a magistrate executing the incurable, not of private killing.

rows.original: silens quietaque totas domus funditus tollit et familias rei publicae pestilentes cum coniugibus ac liberis perdit
rows.translation: Latin (The Latin Library text, CLTK copy), read directly; English is my own close rendering
rows.says: Reason does not rage; but if it must, silently and calmly it removes whole houses root and branch, destroys families dangerous to the state together with wives and children, razes their very houses and wipes out names hostile to liberty, all without the gnashing of teeth that ill becomes a judge.
rows.bearing: Approves, as reason, the state's destruction of families judged dangerous to the state, wives and children included. It is a judge's or the state's act, so it is context only for K1 (exclusion (a), rule 5), and it is not war, so it does not bear on K3. 'tollit' and 'perdit' (remove, destroy) need not mean killing: exile, ruin and confiscation fit too, so as to killing it is Implied. Recorded because it shows that counted texts let public authority punish the relatives of the guilty, which limits how far Letter 95.30 to 95.33 can be read as a rule against all collective killing.

rows.says: At the midday shows the condemned are made to kill one another unarmed for the crowd: 'mere murders'. rows.original: A singulorum deinde caedibus in exitia gentium serpit et inicere tectis ignem, aratrum vetustis urbibus inducere potentiam putat ... multos quidem occidere et indiscretos incendii ac ruinae potentia est
rows.translation: Latin (The Latin Library text, CLTK copy, and Perseus), read directly; English is my own close rendering
rows.says: Cruelty spares not even its own; it creeps from single murders to the destruction of nations, and thinks it power to set roofs on fire and drive the plough over ancient cities; it thinks ordering one or two deaths unworthy of a commander unless a crowd of wretches stands under the blow at once. The crown for saving citizens is a finer ornament for a ruler than arms stripped from the defeated or chariots red with barbarian blood. To save people in crowds is godlike power; to kill many without distinction is the power of fire and collapse.
rows.bearing: Clear teaching, in part, for K3: killing many without distinction, burning cities and destroying peoples are condemned as cruelty, and the blood and spoils of war are ranked below saving lives. It is addressed to a ruler (context for K1, rule 5) and is not framed as a rule of war, so it supports Letter 95.30 to 95.31 rather than carrying K3 alone.

But it names the destroying of 'a human being who has done no wrong' as murder (phonos) and calls that person a citizen of the 'great city', so it supports K1's principle by argument (Implied). K1.label: Contradicted
K1.reason: Deciding text: Seneca, De Ira 1.15.2 (Tier 1; VERIFIED direct in the Latin Library text): 'liberos quoque, si debiles monstrosique editi sunt, mergimus; nec ira sed ratio est a sanis inutilia secernere'. Rule 9: newborns are persons. Rule 4 does not apply: the teacher does not merely report the custom but classes it as 'ratio' (for a Stoic, right action) and uses it as a model for right punishment. Rule 5 does not apply: in Seneca's list the drowning of 'liberos' is an act of parents and households, not a court's sentence or a ruler's order. Stoicism has no branches, so rule 2 applies, not rule 3. Rule 6 does not apply as written: no Stoic counted text, classical commentator or authority narrows the sentence. Epictetus, Discourses 1.23 (Tier 1, verified) teaches against abandoning one's children but opposes rather than narrows Seneca, and does not address weak or deformed infants; Musonius, Lecture 15 dissents but is Tier 2 and unverified. Everyone beyond infancy is protected by directly verified counted texts: Explicit wider rules in Letter 95.51 to 95.52 ('Ut pareamus sanguini humano?'), Letter 95.33 ('Homo, sacra res homini') and De Ira 2.31.7 ('ergo et homini'); Clear teaching for wrongdoers (Meditations 2.1; Epictetus 1.18), slaves (De Clementia 1.18; De Ira 3.40), sons (De Clementia 1.15.1) and a tyrant's infant son (De Beneficiis 7.20.1). Other hard texts found do not change the label: De Beneficiis 7.19 to 7.20 approves a tyrant's death only when he is actively killing and past cure (within the exception); De Beneficiis 3.23.5 approves a slave's killing of his captured master as a benefit (war and voluntary-death context, a hard case); De Ira 1.12 names no killing; De Ira 1.19.2 (families destroyed 'with wives and children') is a judge's act, exclusion (a). Caveat: if the project lead reads the clause as public expiation of prodigies ordered by the state (a modern scholarly reading, outside the corpus), the act would not be on a parent's own authority and the label would fall to Unclear. Consistency with the cross-tradition hard cases: the same test is applied as to Numbers 35:26 to 27, Phinehas and Abū Dāwūd 4361 (a counted text says a private killing was right or blameless); the difference is only that Stoicism has no commentator or interpreting body that could narrow the text under rule 6, a structural point the article should state openly.

K0.label: Unclear
K0.reason: Each clause is taught by directly verified counted texts. Anger: De Ira 3.12.7 ('Nihil tibi liceat dum irasceris', Explicit), De Ira 3.40, 3.43.3 to 3.43.5, 1.5.2, Meditations 2.1. Hatred: Meditations 2.1, De Ira 1.15.1 ('sine odio'), Epictetus 1.18.9 ('pity him rather than hate him'). Revenge: De Ira 2.32.1 ('Inhumanum uerbum est ... ultio', Explicit), De Ira 2.31.8, Meditations 6.6, Epictetus 1.28 (Medea). Gain and all other motives: the Explicit wider rules of Letter 95.51 to 95.52 and De Ira 2.31.7. The label is Unclear (rule 6) because of one counted text: De Ira 1.15.2 approves parents drowning weak or deformed newborns, expressly not from anger ('nec ira') or hatred ('sine odio'), in order 'to separate the useless from the sound'. In Seneca's frame the purpose is to protect the sound (the flock analogy), not the parent's profit. If 'for your own gain' means personal profit or advantage, K0 is Taught; if it includes ridding a household of a child judged a burden, K0 is Contradicted (rule 2). The project lead should fix one reading and apply it to every tradition with an approved killing of a 'useless' or 'burdensome' person. Not deciding: De Ira 1.12 ('exequar') names no killing and is read within the treatise against revenge (2.31.8, 2.32.1); De Beneficiis 7.19 to 7.20 falls within the exception; De Beneficiis 3.23.5 is motivated by the victim's supposed good; Cicero, De Officiis 1.20 is Tier 2.

K3.label: Taught
K3.reason: Taught through a wider rule (rule 7 applied to the war wording). Letter 95.30 to 95.31 (Tier 1, VERIFIED direct) condemns wars and 'occisarum gentium gloriosum scelus', the 'glorious crime' of slaughtering whole peoples, which takes in children, the old and other non-combatants, and complains that deeds punished with death in private persons are praised in generals: Clear teaching. De Clementia 1.26.4 to 1.26.5 (Tier 1, VERIFIED direct) condemns cruelty that moves from single murders to the destruction of nations and the burning of cities, and says 'to kill many without distinction is the power of fire and collapse': Clear teaching in part, addressed to a ruler. Implied only: De Clementia 1.18.1 ('parcere etiam captivis', said of slaves) and Meditations 10.10 (glory in capturing Sarmatians likened to robbery). No counted Stoic text approves killing non-combatants in war. De Ira 1.19.2 (the state destroying families 'with wives and children') is judicial, not war, and is Implied as to killing. Cicero, De Officiis 1.34 to 1.35 (Tier 2, unverified) protects those who surrender but approves razing Carthage and Numantia; not counted. Caveat: no counted text states non-combatant immunity as such; the label rests on a wider condemnation, credited in the same way as wider rules elsewhere. K3 is a record wording; war is context only for K1 (rule 5).

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The rule 4 step rests partly on the claim that Seneca 'uses it as a model for right punishment'. That is presupposing: an analogy draws its force from the hearer already accepting a practice, and rule 4 says presupposing does not decide. The best case for a gentler label goes further. It says that 'nec ira sed ratio est' only classifies the motive (cool calculation, not passion) and does not call the act right, so the whole clause would be Implied. That case fails, but only because of the text itself, not the bare claim that 'ratio' means right action for a Stoic. In the same treatise, reason is the norm and not a neutral faculty: 'satis nos instruxit ratione natura' (1.17.2) and 'Ratio id iudicare uult quod aequum est' (1.18.1), both read directly in the CLTK Latin Library copy. 'a sanis inutilia secernere' is also stated as a general maxim, not as a report of what Romans do. 'Non est illa ira, sed misera curatio' (1.15.2) calls such removal a wretched cure: regretted, but still a cure.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 4: presupposing does not decide, but the teacher's own verdict does. Rule 2.
objections.proposed: Rest the rule 4 step only on 'nec ira sed ratio est a sanis inutilia secernere', read with De Ira 1.17.2 and 1.18.1. Drop 'uses it as a model' as a ground, and drop 'for a Stoic, right action' as an unsupported assertion. Label unchanged.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The reason says 'Rule 6 does not apply as written' because no Stoic text, commentator or authority narrows the sentence. That answers only one of rule 6's three triggers, the narrowing reading. The other two are 'a disputed word' and 'a hard case such as a killing whose judicial or private character is disputed'. Neither is limited to the tradition's own authorities. The public-expiation reading in the caveat is exactly that kind of dispute, and the verb gives it some grip. The rows' own context row (Livy 27.37, unverified) records infants judged to be prodigies being drowned on public order, and 'portentosos' and 'monstrosique' are prodigy words. Three points still decide against it for now. (i) The rows name no scholar or work for this reading, so it is an unverified claim and cannot move a label (rule 1, by analogy with unverified texts). (ii) The sentence itself points to private practice. 'liberos' means children in relation to their parents. 'quoque' marks a step from 'fetus' (the usual word for animal young, in a list of animals) to human children. 'debiles' (weak) is not a prodigy category. And the first person plural sits in a list of owners' own acts (mad dogs, an untamable ox, sick sheep). (iii) Even on the public reading, the drowning is not a punishment, so exclusion (a) as worded ('punishment imposed through a court or a ruler') would not cover it. It would fall outside K1 only through K1's scope clause, 'acting on their own authority'.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 6 (all three triggers). Rule 5 (dispute over judicial or private character). Rule 1 (unverified material never decides). The wording of exclusion (a) and of K1's scope clause.
objections.proposed: Keep Contradicted, and rewrite the caveat. The label would fall to Unclear under rule 6 (disputed word or hard case) only if both of these hold: a named and verified scholarly source shows that 'liberos ... mergimus' refers to public expiation, and the project lead reads K1's 'own authority' clause as leaving a non-punitive killing by public order outside the floor. Also state the textual reasons above that favour the private reading.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The De Beneficiis 3.23.5 row calls the Vettius killing a hard case partly because 'the setting is war (exclusion (b))'. Exclusion (b) covers war between communities or states. A slave killing his own captured master with a seized sword is not an act of war by one community against another; the war is only the setting. The only real ground for a hard case is exclusion (d), and (d) as written covers 'the end of one's own life'. Read directly in Perseus, the text gives the slave's own initiative ('primum dominum occidit ... iam dominum manu misi') and Seneca's verdict ('Da mihi quemquam, qui magnificentius dominum servaverit'). It says nothing of Vettius asking to die. So this is a counted text approving a private person's deliberate killing of someone who threatened no one. Only presumed consent keeps it from being a contradiction, which makes it a hard case of the same kind as the annex's 'without stated consent'. This matters for how firm the result is. If De Ira 1.15.2 were ever moved to Unclear, K1 would still not be Taught, because this text holds it at Unclear on its own.
objections.rule_basis: Exclusions (b) and (d). Rule 2. Rule 6 (hard case the wording does not plainly cover).
objections.proposed: Drop the war ground. Record the text as a second candidate deciding text, Unclear on its own (a mercy killing with consent presumed, not stated), and say that it keeps K1 from Taught whatever happens to De Ira 1.15.2.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The strongest case that Contradicted is too harsh runs like this. Stoicism is a school of several teachers. A later Tier 1 teacher, Epictetus, teaches against casting away one's own offspring (Discourses 1.23, 'οὐκ ἄν σε ἔρριψαν') and against treating common parental practice as right (1.11). Musonius (Tier 2) argues against exposure. So one sentence of Seneca should not speak for the whole school. Under the rules this fails. Epictetus opposes Seneca's sentence rather than narrowing it, and does not discuss weak or deformed infants. Rule 2 needs only one counted text that approves. METHOD section 9, decision 7 says later authorities never outweigh a contradicting counted text. Corpus.md also shows that Seneca's moral essays were added to Tier 1 and approved (decision 11) before any article was tested, so the result does not come from a rule changed for this article.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 2. Rule 6 (opposing a text is not narrowing it). METHOD section 9, decisions 7 and 11.
objections.proposed: Keep Contradicted. Say openly in the article that the school is divided on this: Seneca approves; Epictetus opposes in spirit; Musonius opposes but is not counted. Also say that the label follows from one approving counted text.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The Article I annex's rule 2 counts as Contradicted 'a text that treats a harm as within a master's or parent's proper power while faulting only how it is done (in haste, in anger, to excess)'. The Article II brief says its rules mirror the annex, but its rule 2 leaves this clause out. De Ira 3.32.1 to 3.32.2 (read directly) is such a text for masters. 'non peribit potestas ista, si differetur' treats the power as one the master keeps. 'ad ferrum uenimus, ad capitalia supplicia ... rem castigandam flagris leuioribus' faults masters' capital punishments only as too much for small faults. De Ira 3.40 (death for a broken cup) and De Clementia 1.18.2 ('est aliquid', only some things are forbidden against a slave) likewise fault the cause or the cruelty, not the power. Under the brief as written these are presupposition (rule 4) and Implied, and the Explicit wider rules reach slaves, so 'everyone beyond infancy is protected' holds. Under the annex clause, De Ira 3.32.2 would be a second, separate contradiction for slaves.
objections.rule_basis: Brief rules 2 and 4, compared with Article I annex rule 2.
objections.proposed: Record that under the brief's rule 2 these texts are Implied. Ask the project lead whether the annex clause carries over to Article II. If it does, add De Ira 3.32.2 as a further Contradicted ground (slaves). The label is unchanged either way.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The English of the deciding row is the researcher's own rendering. translations.md names Aubrey Stewart (1889) for the moral essays, and no row has read it. The label turns on 'ratio', 'inutilia' and 'liberos', and the translation of these words can change how strongly the sentence reads.
objections.proposed: Check Stewart's English for De Ira 1.15.2 before the article quotes it. Add 'ratio', 'inutilia' and 'liberos' to 'Where translation changes meaning' in translations.md.

objections.label: K0
objections.objection: The reason grounds Unclear in rule 6 but does not say which trigger applies. The text's meaning is not in doubt; what is undetermined is K0's own word 'gain'. That is rule 6's hard-case trigger (a case the wording does not plainly cover), as in the annex's rule 6. The strongest case for Taught: K0 names four motives. Seneca states his own motive, which is reason, separating the useless from the sound, in a frame where removal is said to help even the one removed ('cui tum maxime prosum cum illum sibi eripio', 1.15.2). He expressly denies two of the four (anger and hatred). 'Gain' is never mentioned, and reading it in is an inference, which is Implied. The strongest case for Contradicted: the flock analogy (sick sheep killed 'ne gregem polluant') protects the sound only where the one removed could infect them. A weak newborn threatens no one, so 'inutilia' can only mean of no use to the household, and drowning the child is ridding oneself of a burden. The uncounted Stoic voices (Musonius, Lecture 15; Hierocles) also treat getting rid of children as a matter of wealth. Neither case settles the question on the text.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 6 (hard case the wording does not plainly cover). Rule 4 (an inferred motive is Implied). Rule 1 (Musonius and Hierocles do not decide).
objections.proposed: Keep Unclear and name the trigger. The project lead should decide whether 'gain' includes ridding oneself or one's household of a dependant judged useless or a burden, and apply that reading in every tradition.

objections.label: K0
objections.objection: The corrections say that De Ira 1.12 'no longer bears on' K0, because the treatise's own texts (2.31.8 and 2.32.1) narrow it. Under rule 6, a reading that the tradition's own counted texts narrow makes a result Unclear; it does not remove the hard text. Read directly, 1.12 approves dutiful retribution for a father struck down. 'Non irascetur, sed uindicabit' (1.12.1). 'caesus est: exequar, quia oportet, non quia dolet' (1.12.2). And 1.12.5 says anger is 'uindicandi cupidior' and for that very reason 'ad uindicandum inhabilis', which implies that avenging is a proper act when reason does it. In this setting, a son seeing his father 'caedi' and his mother 'rapi', 'caedi' most naturally means slain. Neither the means (lethal or not) nor the route (a court or one's own hand) is stated. Seneca rejects 'ultio' (2.32.1) but approves 'uindicare'. Whether dutiful, unangry retribution for a past killing counts as 'revenge' in K0's sense is a hard case. It does not change the present label, but it changes the conditional one. If the project lead reads 'gain' narrowly, K0 would still be Unclear because of 1.12, not Taught, unless the lead rules that 1.12 names no killing and is only Implied.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 6 (narrowing by the tradition's own counted texts; disputed word; hard case). Rule 5 (whether the act is judicial or private is not stated).
objections.proposed: Restore De Ira 1.12 as a second ground for Unclear on the revenge clause. Record 2.31.8 and 2.32.1 as the tradition's own narrowing, and state both conditional outcomes.

objections.label: K0
objections.objection: Several texts are missing or under-used. (1) Letter 95.30, 'Non avaritia, non crudelitas modum novit' (read directly in Perseus), comes straight after murders and wars and names greed and cruelty as what drives them. It is Clear teaching for the gain clause, but the reason supports 'gain' only through wider rules. (2) De Ira 3.14.4 ('o dignum in quem omnium suorum arcus uerterentur', said of Cambyses) and 3.15.2 ('non ueto quaerere dignam tam truci portento poenam'), both read directly, say that a king who killed a man's son deserves death or a fitting penalty. One is an exclamation and the other a concession; no killing is approved, and each king is an ongoing killer, which brings in the exception. Implied. (3) De Beneficiis 7.19.9 admits that the tyrant becomes 'invisum mihi' (hateful to me) before Seneca approves his death. This falls within the exception.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 7. Rule 4. The exception in K0.
objections.proposed: Add Letter 95.30 as Clear teaching for the gain clause. Record De Ira 3.14.4, De Ira 3.15.2 and De Beneficiis 7.19.9 as limits (Implied, or within the exception). No label change.

objections.label: K3
objections.objection: The reason reads Letter 95.30 to 95.31 as condemning 'wars'. In the same letter, Seneca gives 'Sciet pro patria pugnandum esse' (95.37 in Perseus numbering, read directly) as a precept everyone knows. Letter 66.13 (read directly) calls Scipio 'magnus' for blockading Numantia and forcing its unconquered people to turn their hands on themselves, and De Ira 1.11.7 (read directly) praises the same siege for its patience. So the counted texts accept fighting for one's country, and 95.30 to 95.31 cannot be a wider rule against all killing in war. What it does teach clearly is narrower: wars driven by greed and cruelty ('Non avaritia, non crudelitas modum novit') and the slaughter of whole peoples ('occisarum gentium gloriosum scelus') are crimes. The counted text closest to the principle of distinction is De Clementia 1.26.5, 'multos quidem occidere et indiscretos', killing many without distinction. The reason quotes it but does not use it for this point.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 7 (a wider rule must actually be taught as a rule). Rule 4.
objections.proposed: Rest K3 on three things: (i) the slaughter of whole peoples (Letter 95.30 to 95.31); (ii) indiscriminate killing (De Clementia 1.26.4 to 1.26.5); (iii) the Explicit wider rules (Letter 95.51 to 95.52, 95.33; De Ira 2.31.7), which the tradition limits for fighting but nowhere for those who do not fight. Record Letter 95.37, Letter 66.13 and De Ira 1.11.7 as limits.

objections.label: K3
objections.objection: The strongest case for 'Taught in part': no counted text addresses the deliberate killing of individual non-combatants or of those who have surrendered. De Clementia 1.18.1 ('parcere etiam captivis') is about slaves and is only Implied. The two Clear texts condemn mass and indiscriminate killing. The Article I annex's rule 7 says that for L2 and L3 a wider duty does not count on its own where a tradition teaches the wider duty and accepts the practice in the same texts. By analogy, the wider rules should not carry war, since Seneca accepts fighting (95.37). That would make K3 'Taught in part'. This fails, but only narrowly. The annex restriction applies where the counted texts accept the very practice under test. Here they accept fighting, not the killing of people who are not fighting, and no counted text accepts that. So the wider rules still reach non-combatants, and they reach those who have surrendered, who are no longer fighting.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 7 (wider rules; taught in part). Analogy with Article I annex rule 7.
objections.proposed: Keep Taught, marked as at the lower edge. Record that the surrendered and individual non-combatants rest only on wider rules and Implied texts. If the project lead applies the annex's L2 and L3 reasoning to war, the label becomes Taught in part: the slaughter of peoples and indiscriminate killing are taught, but the protection of the surrendered and of individual non-combatants is not.

objections.label: K3
objections.objection: The strongest case that Taught is too gentle is Letter 66.13. Seneca praises as great the general who starved Numantia until its people killed themselves, a method that by its nature kills non-combatants. Under the rules it is Implied. No non-combatant is named. The deaths are by the besieged's own hands, so 'deliberately kill' is not met on the text. And what is praised is the equality of the virtues (the besieger's persistence and the besieged's endurance), not the deaths. De Ira 1.11.7 is the same.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 4. Rule 6 (not a hard case on the text, because no deliberate killing of non-combatants is approved).
objections.proposed: Add rows for Letter 66.13 and De Ira 1.11.7 (context: war; Implied for K3) as limits. No label change.

K1.label: Contradicted
K1.reason: Deciding text: Seneca, De Ira 1.15.2 (Tier 1; VERIFIED direct, CLTK Latin Library copy; read again in this check): 'liberos quoque, si debiles monstrosique editi sunt, mergimus; nec ira sed ratio est a sanis inutilia secernere'. Rule 9: the victims are newborns, so they are persons. Rule 4 is met by the teacher's own verdict, 'nec ira sed ratio est'. In this treatise reason is the norm ('satis nos instruxit ratione natura', 1.17.2; 'Ratio id iudicare uult quod aequum est', 1.18.1), and the clause states a general maxim, not a report of custom. The analogy's use as a model for punishment is not relied on. Rule 5: the clause describes acts by households ('liberos'; 'quoque' marking the step from animal young to children; 'debiles', which is not a prodigy category; the first person plural in a list of owners' own acts). It is not a punishment, so exclusion (a) does not apply. There are no branches, so rule 2 applies, not rule 3. Rule 6: none of its three triggers is met on present evidence. No counted text, commentator or authority narrows the clause. Epictetus, Discourses 1.23 and 1.11 oppose it in spirit but do not narrow it, and decision 7 says later authorities never outweigh a contradicting counted text. The public-expiation reading has no named, verified source in the rows. If such a source is verified, and the project lead reads K1's 'own authority' clause as leaving a non-punitive killing by public order outside the floor, the label falls to Unclear, not to Taught. That is because De Beneficiis 3.23.5 (a slave's approved killing of his captured master, consent unstated) is an independent hard case under rule 6. Its ground is exclusion (d) and presumed consent, not war. De Ira 1.12 is a further hard case if read as a private, lethal 'exequar'. All other classes beyond infancy are protected by Explicit wider rules (Letter 95.51 to 95.52, 95.33; De Ira 2.31.7) and by Clear teaching (Meditations 2.1; Epictetus 1.18; De Clementia 1.18; De Ira 3.40; De Clementia 1.15.1; De Beneficiis 7.20.1). De Beneficiis 7.19 to 7.20 falls within the exception. De Ira 1.19.2 is judicial. De Ira 3.32.2 presupposes masters' capital punishments and faults only excess, so it is Implied under the brief's rule 4; under the annex's rule 2 clause it would be a second contradiction for slaves.

K0.label: Unclear
K0.reason: Rule 6, hard-case trigger: the case is one that K0's undefined word 'gain' does not plainly cover. Every clause of K0 is taught by directly verified counted texts. Anger: De Ira 3.12.7 ('Nihil tibi liceat dum irasceris', Explicit), 1.5.2, 3.40 and 3.43.3 to 3.43.5. Hatred: Meditations 2.1; De Ira 1.15.1 ('sine odio'); Epictetus 1.18. Revenge: De Ira 2.32.1 ('Inhumanum uerbum est ... ultio', Explicit), 2.31.8; Meditations 6.6; Epictetus 1.28. Gain: Letter 95.30 ('Non avaritia, non crudelitas modum novit', Clear teaching), together with the Explicit wider rules of Letter 95.51 to 95.52 and De Ira 2.31.7. The first ground for Unclear is De Ira 1.15.2. It approves parents drowning weak or deformed newborns, expressly not from anger or hatred, in order 'a sanis inutilia secernere'. Whether ridding a household of a child judged useless is killing 'for your own gain' turns on K0's wording, not on the text. If the project lead reads 'gain' as personal profit or advantage, this ground falls away. If 'gain' includes ridding oneself of a burden, K0 is Contradicted under rule 2. The second ground is De Ira 1.12 ('uindicabit'; 'caesus est: exequar, quia oportet'; anger is 'ad uindicandum inhabilis'). This approves dutiful, unangry retribution for a slain father; neither the means nor the route is stated. The treatise's own texts (2.31.8, 2.32.1) narrow it, and under rule 6 a narrowed reading gives Unclear, not removal. So even on a narrow reading of 'gain', K0 stays Unclear, unless the lead rules that 1.12 names no killing and is only Implied. De Beneficiis 7.19 to 7.20 is within the exception. De Beneficiis 3.23.5 is motivated by the victim's supposed good. De Ira 3.14.4 and 3.15.2 are an exclamation and a concession, so they are Implied. Cicero, De Officiis 1.20 is Tier 2 and is not counted.

K3.label: Taught
K3.reason: Taught, at the lower edge. Clear teaching that the slaughter of whole peoples is a crime: Letter 95.30 to 95.31, 'occisarum gentium gloriosum scelus', together with 'Non avaritia, non crudelitas modum novit'. Clear teaching, in part and addressed to a ruler, that killing many without distinction is cruelty: De Clementia 1.26.4 to 1.26.5, 'multos quidem occidere et indiscretos'. Both take in children, the old and civilians. These sit beside the Explicit wider rules (Letter 95.51 to 95.52; 95.33; De Ira 2.31.7), which the counted texts limit for fighting ('pro patria pugnandum esse', Letter 95.37) but nowhere for those who are not fighting. No counted Stoic text approves the deliberate killing of non-combatants or of those who have surrendered. Letter 95.30 to 95.31 is not a condemnation of war as such, because Letter 95.37, Letter 66.13 and De Ira 1.11.7 accept or praise fighting and siege. Letter 66.13 and De Ira 1.11.7 praise Scipio's siege of Numantia, but name no non-combatant, and the deaths there were by the besieged's own hands, so they are Implied limits. The surrendered and individual non-combatants rest only on wider rules and Implied texts: De Clementia 1.18.1 ('parcere etiam captivis', said of slaves) and Meditations 10.10. If the project lead applies the Article I annex's L2 and L3 reasoning on wider rules to war, the label becomes Taught in part. De Ira 1.19.2 is judicial and not war. Cicero, De Officiis 1.34 to 1.35 is Tier 2 and unverified.

challenge.consistency_notes: The same test is applied to Stoicism as to the other hard cases: a counted text whose teacher says a private killing was right or blameless contradicts K1, unless rule 5 or rule 6 applies. The difference is not only structural. Seneca, De Ira 1.15.2 is among the plainest texts on the list. It gives the teacher's own verdict as a general maxim ('nec ira sed ratio est'). It is not a narrative of zeal later read narrowly, as with Phinehas (Numbers 25 and Psalm 106:30 to 31), where a rabbinic narrowing can trigger rule 6. It is not a ruler's ruling after the event, as with Abū Dāwūd 4361, where the Prophet's role as ruler can raise a rule 5 question. It is not the killing of someone a court has already judged, as with Numbers 35:26 to 27. It names a class of victims squarely inside K1 under rule 9. And no counted text, commentator or authorised body narrows it. So if any of those cases is labelled Contradicted, Stoicism must be too. If they are labelled Unclear, it should be because of a rule 5 or rule 6 feature that Seneca's text lacks. The only such feature here is the public-expiation reading, which has no source in the rows. The structural point should still be stated openly: a tradition with no living interpreters cannot be rescued by narrowing, and opposing teaching by a later teacher (Epictetus) does not count as narrowing under rule 6 or decision 7. The same rule must hold for the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Mahāyāna Buddhism), Yasna 31.18 and 33.2 (Zoroastrianism), and the Atharvaveda rites and Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.4.12 (Hinduism). Opposing passages elsewhere in those traditions do not soften an approving counted text unless they narrow its reach. For K0, the project lead's reading of 'gain' must be applied in the same way to every tradition with an approved killing of a dependant judged useless or a burden. The rule 6 treatment of De Ira 1.12 (an approving text narrowed by the tradition's own counted texts gives Unclear, not removal) must match how Phinehas and Sanhedrin 82a are treated for Judaism. For K3, crediting Seneca's condemnations of the slaughter of peoples and of indiscriminate killing as Clear teaching is consistent only if similar wider condemnations of war in other traditions are credited the same way. The rule for wider rules in war (whether the Article I annex's L2 and L3 restriction applies) must be fixed once for all thirteen traditions. Finally, the Article II brief's rule 2 omits the annex's clause on 'faulting only how it is done'. Whether that omission is deliberate affects masters' texts in Stoicism (De Ira 3.32.2) and probably in other traditions, so the project lead should settle it for all of them.
